name: Beaver
lede: Beaver is a light, greyish reddish brown named for the animal's fur, a color tied to the fur trade, when Europeans coveted beaver pelts for their hat industry.

sections.title: Named for the animal
sections.body:
Beaver is a plain animal name: the color of beaver fur [1]. Paterson's dictionary lists it among the browns, and in the same book the adjective beaver-hued means colored like the animal [1]. The color also appears under that name in the Crayola list and in the ISCC-NBS system of 1955, where this swatch sits in the block called light grayish reddish brown, about 2.3 units away [2].

The neighbors are quiet and earthy: [[taupe]], [[fawn]], [[mushroom]] and [[beige]] all sit near it in lightness and chroma [2].

sections.title: Beaver, the hat and the trade
sections.body:
Europeans coveted beaver pelts for their hat industry, and Native North Americans bartered for them with English woolens dyed with tin and cochineal scarlet [3]. So a scarlet cloth of the fur trade was exchanged for the fur behind this brown [3].

Beaver is also used in a related word. Paterson's entry for the color castor describes a dark brownish grey or light brown beaver color, and notes that the name was hoped to come from the star Castor and not from the animal's scent gland [1]. Paterson does not say how the two names are linked, and our sources leave it unresolved [1].

sections.title: Beaver as a soft brown
sections.body:
Derek Jarman's *Chroma* finds nostalgia in brown and remembers his mother's soft beaver lamb coat, in which the family buried their tears [4]. That use is personal rather than historical [4].

The swatch is a light brown with a pink-orange cast, between [[brown]] and [[taupe]] in feel [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 748 works, or 3.2 per cent, more common than 82 per cent of the named colors [5]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 4.5 per cent of the paintings from that century [5]. It is far more common in South Asian painting than in Europe: the Nepal lift is 6.5 times the baseline, India 2.5 and Japan 1.9, with Pahari and Mughal painting leading [6].

The likely explanation is the ground of the paper, silk and cloth, not a deliberate beaver color [6]. As always these are photographs of aged paintings, so the colors are as photographed [5].
